title: Topic Drill: Sentence Structure, Grammar and Punctuation (Set D)

items.stem:
The Harlow College career fair opens Thursday in the gymnasium. A volunteer drafted the floor-plan notice for the student newsletter and asked a classmate to proofread it. One sentence in the draft reads: Behind the registration tables is a row of employer booths and a bank of charging stations.

Which revision corrects the sentence in the draft?
options: Behind the registration tables is a row of employer booths, and a bank of charging stations.
Behind the registration tables were a row of employer booths and a bank of charging stations.
Behind the registration tables be a row of employer booths and a bank of charging stations.
Behind the registration tables are a row of employer booths and a bank of charging stations.
items.explanation: In an inverted sentence the subject follows the verb. The compound subject a row of employer booths and a bank of charging stations is plural, so the verb must be are. The original is keeps a singular verb. Adding a comma still leaves is, and were shifts the tense away from the present tense of the notice.

items.stem:
Maribel is helping a friend polish a cover letter for a booth at the Harlow career fair. The friend is applying to a regional hospital’s billing office. The letter says: Mr. Ostrander met with Mr. Pell before he interviewed the candidates.

Which revision removes the unclear pronoun reference?
options: Mr. Ostrander met with Mr. Pell before he himself interviewed the candidates.
Mr. Ostrander met with Mr. Pell before they interviewed the candidates.
Before interviewing the candidates, Mr. Ostrander met with Mr. Pell.
Mr. Ostrander met with Mr. Pell before the other man interviewed the candidates.
items.explanation: The pronoun he could refer to either man, so the reader cannot tell who interviewed the candidates. Rewriting with the introductory phrase before interviewing names Mr. Ostrander as the doer. Adding himself, switching to they, or calling Mr. Pell the other man leaves the meaning unclear or changes who did what.

items.stem:
A career services office posted tips for students preparing to attend the Harlow fair. One tip in the draft handout reads: Walking into the crowded gym, the line for the accounting firm looked far too long.

Which revision corrects the modifier problem in the tip?
options: Walking into the crowded gym, the long line for the accounting firm looked far too long to us.
Walking into the crowded gym, we thought the line for the accounting firm looked far too long.
Walking into the crowded gym, the line for the accounting firm, it looked far too long.
Walking into the crowded gym, a line for the accounting firm was looked at as far too long.
items.explanation: The opening phrase walking into the crowded gym needs a person as the subject, but the line cannot walk. Putting we right after the comma fixes the dangling participle. The other revisions still make a line or a vague it the subject, or turn the verb into an awkward passive.

items.stem:
At the Harlow career fair, the placement director gave students advice about choosing which employers to approach first. A handout excerpt says: Students should either research each employer before the fair or they should arrive early to read the company displays.

Which revision makes the sentence parallel?
options: Students should either research each employer before the fair or arrive early to read the company displays.
Students should either research each employer before the fair or they arrive early to read the company displays.
Students should either research each employer before the fair or to arrive early and read the company displays.
Students should research each employer before the fair or else arrival early to read the company displays.
items.explanation: Either and or must introduce matching grammatical parts. Here either is followed by the verb phrase research each employer, so or should be followed by another verb phrase, arrive early. The original pairs a verb phrase with a full clause. The other options pair a verb with an infinitive or with the noun arrival.

items.stem:
A first-year student wrote a reflection on her first day at the Harlow career fair for the campus magazine. She described the crowded aisle outside the gym. Her draft reads: She walked past a loud crowded aisle toward the engineering booths.

Where should a comma be added?
options: She walked, past a loud crowded aisle toward the engineering booths.
She walked past a loud, crowded aisle toward the engineering booths.
She walked past a loud crowded, aisle toward the engineering booths.
She walked past a loud crowded aisle, toward the engineering booths.
items.explanation: Loud and crowded are coordinate adjectives, because each describes aisle on its own and could be joined by and, so a comma separates them. A comma after the verb, after the last adjective, or before the prepositional phrase would split the sentence at points where no pause or list is intended.

items.stem:
The Eastgate library runs a volunteer tutoring program for middle school readers. The coordinator wrote a thank-you email to the helpers. She typed: The tutors who arrives early on Tuesdays sets out the books and pencils.

Which revision corrects the subject-verb agreement?
options: The tutors who arrive early on Tuesdays set out the books and pencils.
The tutors who arrive early on Tuesdays sets out the books and pencils.
The tutors who arrives early on Tuesdays set out the books and pencils.
The tutors who arrive early on Tuesdays has set out the books and pencils.
items.explanation: The subject tutors is plural, and the relative pronoun who takes the same number, so both verbs must be plural: arrive and set. The other choices fix only one verb and leave the other singular, or replace set with has set, which is a singular helping verb that still does not agree with tutors.

items.stem:
Eastgate library tutors keep a daily log of what each student practiced. A volunteer reviewing the log noticed an awkward line in a report to parents. It reads: Last week, Dario reads two chapters aloud and then he summarized them without help.

Which revision uses consistent verb tense?
options: Last week, Dario reads two chapters aloud and then summarizes them without help.
Last week, Dario read two chapters aloud and then he summarizes them without help.
Last week, Dario read two chapters aloud and then summarized them without help.
Last week, Dario had read two chapters aloud and then summarizes them without help.
items.explanation: The phrase last week places both actions in the past, so read and summarized should both be past tense. The first revision makes both verbs present, which conflicts with last week. The other two mix past or past perfect with a present verb, so the sequence of events stays inconsistent.

items.stem:
Tutors at the Eastgate library were asked to explain a new rule about borrowing reading kits. A flyer for the program says: Students may borrow the kit for two weeks, however, they must return it before the next session.

Which revision corrects the punctuation in the flyer?
options: Students may borrow the kit for two weeks, however they must return it before the next session.
Students may borrow the kit for two weeks however, they must return it before the next session.
Students may borrow the kit for two weeks; however they, must return it before the next session.
Students may borrow the kit for two weeks; however, they must return it before the next session.
items.explanation: However is a conjunctive adverb joining two complete sentences, so it needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it. The original makes a comma splice. The second choice drops the semicolon, and the third puts a comma inside the second clause, between the subject and its verb.

items.stem:
The Eastgate tutoring coordinator wrote a short message asking volunteers to bring snacks for a reading celebration. She wants to say that the children will eat more fruit at the party than they do at school. Her draft says: The children will eat less pieces of fruit at the party than at school.

Which word correctly fills the blank in: The children will eat ___ pieces of fruit at the party than at school?
options: more
fewer
less
much
items.explanation: Her message needs the opposite of the stated meaning, so the party total must be greater, which calls for more. Fewer would be right for countable pieces if she meant a smaller number, but it reverses her point. Less is wrong for countable items, and much does not combine with pieces to compare two amounts.

items.stem:
A tutor at the Eastgate library is writing a reference for a teenage volunteer. She wants to show how reliable he is. Her draft reads: Mr. Teague, who we trusted with the keys, is the volunteer on who the program most depends.

Which revision uses who and whom correctly?
options: Mr. Teague, who we trusted with the keys, is the volunteer on whom the program most depends.
Mr. Teague, whom we trusted with the keys, is the volunteer on who the program most depends.
Mr. Teague, whom we trusted with the keys, is the volunteer on whom the program most depends.
Mr. Teague, who we trusted with the keys, is the volunteer on who the program most depends.
items.explanation: Whom is the object form. We trusted whom is an object of trusted, and on whom follows the preposition on, so both blanks take whom. The other options keep who in one or both places, which would be correct only for a subject doing the action, as in who arrived early.

items.stem:
The city of Marlow is testing a composting pilot on Alder Street. A resident wrote to the council to describe the first month. One sentence reads: The bins on Alder Street, which were delivered in March, was emptied every Friday.

Which revision corrects the sentence?
options: The bins on Alder Street, which was delivered in March, was emptied every Friday.
The bins on Alder Street, which were delivered in March, were emptied every Friday.
The bin on Alder Street, which were delivered in March, were emptied every Friday.
The bins on Alder Street which were delivered in March, were emptied every Friday.
items.explanation: The subject is bins, which is plural, so the main verb must be were emptied, even with a clause between subject and verb. The first choice makes both verbs singular. The second changes the subject to bin but keeps plural verbs. The third drops one comma, leaving the nonessential clause unbalanced.

items.stem:
The Marlow composting pilot sent households a notice about acceptable materials. A draft line says: Residents should put in the bin: eggshells, coffee grounds, and they can add leaves that have fallen.

Which revision makes the list parallel?
options: Residents should put eggshells, coffee grounds, and leaves that have fallen in the bin.
Residents should put in the bin eggshells, coffee grounds, and adding fallen leaves.
Residents should put eggshells, coffee grounds, and also leaves are fine in the bin.
Residents should put eggshells, coffee grounds, and fallen leaves in the bin.
items.explanation: A list should hold items of the same form. Eggshells, coffee grounds, and fallen leaves are all noun phrases, and the revised sentence also places in the bin after them cleanly. The other options add a clause, a participle, or a full statement inside the list, breaking the pattern even when the meaning is still understandable.

items.stem:
A volunteer for the Marlow composting pilot is writing a field note about a damaged bin. She wrote: Leaving its lid open overnight, a raccoon had tipped the compost bin over.

Which question best identifies whether the modifier is placed correctly?
options: Is the word overnight the right choice, since a raccoon usually hunts after dark?
Who or what left the lid open overnight, and does the subject of the main clause match that doer?
Should the phrase tipped over be moved to the front of the sentence?
Is the word compost needed, since the bin is already described as a bin?
items.explanation: A participial phrase must modify the noun nearest to it. Here leaving its lid open seems to describe the raccoon, though the bin lid was likely left open by a person. The question about who did the action finds the dangling or misplaced modifier. The other questions raise style points, not the modifier error.

items.stem:
The Marlow composting pilot posted a reminder on the neighborhood board. The reminder asks neighbors to rinse out the bins at least once a month. The draft reads: Rinsing your bin helps prevent odors, so you should do it regularly, and, it also keeps flies away.

Where does the extra comma appear that should be removed?
options: The comma after odors
The comma after regularly
The comma after and
No comma should be removed
items.explanation: A comma follows a coordinating conjunction only when a nonessential phrase interrupts the sentence, which does not happen here. The comma after and wrongly separates and from the clause it introduces. The commas after odors and regularly are acceptable breaks before so and and, which join full clauses.

items.stem: A reporter covering the Marlow composting pilot is checking quotations from a resident interview. The reporter’s notes include a sentence of dialogue. Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
options: “The smell was never an issue” said Ms. Ramos, “once we started using the lids”.
“The smell was never an issue,” said Ms. Ramos “once we started using the lids.”
“The smell was never an issue”, said Ms. Ramos, “once we started using the lids.”
“The smell was never an issue,” said Ms. Ramos, “once we started using the lids.”
items.explanation: When a speaker tag interrupts one sentence, commas go inside the quotation marks and the tag is set off with commas on both sides. The first choice leaves out the comma after issue and puts the period outside. The second omits the comma after Ramos. The third puts a comma outside the closing quotation marks.

items.stem:
A volunteer society is restoring a vintage tram that once ran along Pelham Quay. The society’s newsletter editor is reviewing a draft report on the first year of work. One line reads: The tram’s wooden seats, which the volunteers sanded by hand, are the pride of the restoration.

What is the best description of the clause which the volunteers sanded by hand?
options: It is nonessential, so the commas are correct.
It is essential, so the commas should be removed.
It is essential, so which should be changed to that.
It is a fragment, so it should be a separate sentence.
items.explanation: The clause adds extra detail about the seats, but the sentence still identifies them without it, so it is nonrestrictive and takes commas and the word which. An essential clause would use that and no commas. The clause is attached to the main clause, so it is not a fragment.

items.stem:
The Pelham Quay tram society sells postcards to pay for new brass fittings. The treasurer wrote a note thanking donors. It says: The volunteers worked hard this winter, the tram’s paint finally looks fresh.

Which choice best identifies what is wrong with this sentence?
options: It is a fragment missing a subject and a verb.
It is correct because a comma may join two complete sentences.
It needs an apostrophe in volunteers to show possession.
It is a run-on with a comma splice joining two complete thoughts.
items.explanation: Each half of the sentence could stand alone, and only a comma joins them, which is a comma splice. A semicolon, a period, or a conjunction such as and would fix it. The sentence is not a fragment, a comma alone cannot join two sentences, and volunteers here is a plain plural.

items.stem:
A guide leads small tours through the Pelham Quay tram depot on Saturdays. Her script is being checked for a school group visit. A sentence in it reads: Visitors may touch any part of the tram accept the polished control panel.

Which word should replace accept?
options: expect
except
excepting
accepted
items.explanation: Except means excluding, which is the sense needed to say that the control panel may not be touched. Accept means to receive. Expect and accepted are different words, and excepting would make the clause an awkward participle. Only except fits the meaning and the grammar of the sentence.

items.stem:
The Pelham Quay society is preparing a short formal letter to the mayor asking for a grant. A volunteer drafted this sentence: We would really appreciate it a whole lot if you could kinda help us fix up the old tram.

Which revision best fits the formal tone of a letter to a public official?
options: We would greatly appreciate your assistance in restoring the historic tram.
We would really appreciate it a lot if you could help us fix up the tram.
We would be so glad if you could kind of help us with the old tram project.
We would totally love any help you can give us for the tram restoration.
items.explanation: A letter to an official calls for precise, polished wording. The key replaces slang and filler such as kinda and a whole lot with greatly appreciate and assistance. The other choices keep casual phrases such as a lot, so glad, kind of, and totally, which lower the formality of the request.

items.stem:
The tram society is writing a plaque for its restored car. The plaque draft says: The tram was lain in the depot for forty years before volunteers began to restore it.

Which revision uses the correct verb form?
options: The tram laid in the depot for forty years before volunteers began to restore it.
The tram lain in the depot for forty years before volunteers began to restore it.
The tram lay in the depot for forty years before volunteers began to restore it.
The tram was laying in the depot for forty years before volunteers began to restore it.
items.explanation: Lie means to rest, and its past tense is lay, so the tram lay in the depot. Laid is the past tense of lay, which needs an object. Lain is a past participle that needs a helping verb, and was laying is both a wrong form and the wrong tense for a completed period of forty years.

items.stem:
A student council at Wexley Middle School surveyed classmates about school lunches. The council secretary is polishing the summary for the school paper. A line in it says: The survey results shows that most of the students prefers the hot lunch.

Which revision corrects both agreement errors?
options: The survey results shows that most of the students prefer the hot lunch.
The survey results show that most of the students prefer the hot lunch.
The survey results show that most of the students prefers the hot lunch.
The survey results is showing that most of the students prefers the hot lunch.
items.explanation: Results is plural and takes show. In most of the students, the word students is plural, so the verb prefer must be plural too. The other options fix only one verb or replace show with a singular form, so at least one subject and verb still disagree.

items.stem:
The Wexley student council is writing a short history of school lunch for the yearbook. The treasurer found old records and wrote a note for the council minutes. It says: In the 1990’s the council counted fewer than 200 lunches per week, but now it counts nearly 400.

Which revision uses apostrophes and plurals correctly?
options: In the 1990s’ the council counted fewer than 200 lunches per week, but now it counts nearly 400.
In the 1990’s the council counted fewer than 200 lunch’s per week, but now it counts nearly 400.
In the 1990s the council counted fewer than 200 lunchs per week, but now it counts nearly 400.
In the 1990s the council counted fewer than 200 lunches per week, but now it counts nearly 400.
items.explanation: A decade written as numerals forms its plural with an s only, so 1990s needs no apostrophe. An apostrophe signals possession or a contraction, neither of which is intended. The distractors keep an unnecessary apostrophe in the decade, turn lunches into lunch’s, or misspell the plural as lunchs.

items.stem:
The Wexley lunch survey asked students to rank three new menu ideas. A council member drafted a sentence for the results page. It reads: Students liked the pasta bar better then the sandwich station.

Which word should replace then?
options: than
that
when
though
items.explanation: Than is used to compare two things, as in better than. Then refers to time or sequence, which is the error in the draft. That, when, and though do not introduce a comparison, so the only word that produces a correct and logical sentence is than.

items.stem:
The Wexley student council is combining findings from its lunch survey into one sentence. The two sentences to combine are: Most students finish their fruit. Many students leave their vegetables behind.

Which revision best combines the sentences?
options: Most students finish their fruit, many leave their vegetables behind.
Most students finish their fruit, because many leave their vegetables behind.
Most students finish their fruit, but many leave their vegetables behind.
Most students finish their fruit, so many leave their vegetables behind.
items.explanation: The two ideas contrast, so the conjunction but with a comma joins them best. A comma alone makes a splice. Because suggests that leaving vegetables causes finishing fruit, and so suggests a result that is not logical. Only but matches the relationship between the ideas.

items.stem:
The Wexley survey team wrote a closing note for parents about the lunch survey. Part of the note reads: The students enthusiastically cheered with great enthusiasm when the new salad bar was announced.

Which choice best fixes the redundancy?
options: The students cheered enthusiastically with great enthusiasm when the new salad bar opened.
The students cheered with loud enthusiasm and excitement when the new salad bar was announced.
The students enthusiastically cheered with excitement when the new salad bar was announced.
The students cheered enthusiastically when the new salad bar was announced.
items.explanation: Enthusiastically and with great enthusiasm say the same thing twice. Keeping one expression removes the redundancy. The other choices still repeat the idea with enthusiasm and excitement, or pair enthusiastically with with excitement, so the extra words still add nothing new to the meaning, and the sentence stays wordy for readers of the school newsletter.

items.stem:
A coastal erosion study at Tern Point measured how far the cliff edge moved each season. A field assistant wrote the opening of the methods section. It reads: Along the cliff edge runs a series of marker posts that was placed in 2022.

Which revision corrects the agreement error?
options: Along the cliff edge run a series of marker posts that was placed in 2022.
Along the cliff edge runs a series of marker posts that is placed in 2022.
Along the cliff edge runs a series of marker posts that were placed in 2022.
Along the cliff edge runs a series of marker posts that had been placing in 2022.
items.explanation: Marker posts is plural, so the clause that follows needs the plural verb were placed. The main verb runs agrees with the singular subject series, even in inverted order. Changing it to run is unnecessary, is placed does not fit a 2022 date, and had been placing is not a valid form.

items.stem:
The Tern Point erosion study includes a narrative section about a storm that hit the coast. The author wrote: The waves had already undercut the path when the storm will arrive, so the team moved the equipment inland.

Which revision corrects the tense sequence in the sentence?
options: The waves had already undercut the path when the storm arrives, so the team moved the equipment inland.
The waves had already undercut the path when the storm arrived, so the team moved the equipment inland.
The waves already undercut the path when the storm had arrived, so the team moved the equipment inland.
The waves have already undercut the path when the storm arrived, so the team moved the equipment inland.
items.explanation: The storm and the move happened in the past, and the undercutting came earlier still, so past perfect had undercut and simple past arrived are correct together. The other choices pair a present tense with a past event, or reverse the order of the two events, or use a present perfect form.

items.stem:
A researcher on the Tern Point erosion team describes her measurements in a progress report. She wrote: Measuring the cliff retreat each spring, the data showed a loss of nearly two meters.

Which revision corrects the dangling modifier?
options: Measuring the cliff retreat each spring, the team found a loss of nearly two meters.
Measuring the cliff retreat each spring, a loss of nearly two meters was shown by the data.
Measuring the cliff retreat each spring, the data it showed a loss of nearly two meters.
Measuring the cliff retreat each spring, the loss of nearly two meters was found out.
items.explanation: Data cannot measure anything, so the opening phrase dangles. Naming the team right after the comma supplies a doer for measuring. The other choices still give the phrase a non-human subject, such as a loss or the data, or make the sentence awkward without naming who did the measuring.

items.stem:
The Tern Point study ends with recommendations for the town council. One recommendation in a draft reads: The council should neither delay the sea wall repairs nor should it ignore the warnings from the study.

Which revision makes the correlative construction parallel?
options: The council should neither delay the sea wall repairs nor it should ignore the warnings from the study.
The council should not delay the sea wall repairs nor ignoring the warnings from the study.
The council should neither delaying the sea wall repairs nor should ignore the warnings from the study.
The council should neither delay the sea wall repairs nor ignore the warnings from the study.
items.explanation: Neither and nor should be followed by matching forms. Delay the sea wall repairs and ignore the warnings are both verb phrases after the same helping verb should. The other options add a second clause, switch to an ing form, or mix a verb with a participle, which breaks parallelism.

items.stem:
The coastal erosion team at Tern Point collected stories from longtime residents to add context. The editor reviewed one quotation from a fisherman. The sentence reads: “My grandfather always said the sea takes what it wants” the fisherman told us.

What is the correct punctuation for this sentence?
options: “My grandfather always said the sea takes what it wants.” The fisherman told us.
“My grandfather always said the sea takes what it wants”; the fisherman told us.
“My grandfather always said the sea takes what it wants,” the fisherman told us.
“My grandfather always said the sea takes what it wants” the fisherman told us!
items.explanation: When a quotation is followed by a speaker tag, a comma goes inside the closing quotation marks in place of a period. The first option ends the quotation with a period and makes the tag a fragment. The semicolon is outside the marks and misused. The last option omits the comma and adds an exclamation point.

items.stem:
A neighborhood tool swap meets on the first Sunday of each month at the Birchfield community hall. The organizer is writing an announcement for the street association’s page. One sentence in her draft reads: Neither the drills nor the ladder are available for lending this week.

Which revision corrects the agreement error?
options: Neither the drills nor the ladder were available for lending this week.
Neither the drills nor the ladder is available for lending this week.
Neither the drills nor the ladder are available for lending this weekend.
Neither the drills nor the ladders is available for lending this week.
items.explanation: With neither and nor, the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. Ladder is singular, so the verb must be is. The draft uses are, which would suit a plural noun. Were stays plural, and the third option changes the nearest noun to ladders, which would then need are.

items.stem:
The Birchfield tool swap keeps a sign-in sheet so members can track what they borrow. A volunteer wrote a reminder in the hall newsletter. It reads: Please return each tool to it’s labeled shelf before you leave the hall.

Which revision corrects the apostrophe error?
options: Please return each tool to it is labeled shelf before you leave the hall.
Please return each tool to its’ labeled shelf before you leave the hall.
Please return each tool to its labeled shelf before you leave the hall.
Please return each tool’s to its labeled shelf before you leave the hall.
items.explanation: Its without an apostrophe is the possessive form meaning belonging to it. It’s is a contraction of it is, which does not make sense in the sentence. The other options expand the contraction into it is, add a second apostrophe, or make tool possessive without cause, so none repair the error.

items.stem:
The Birchfield tool swap committee is preparing a short guide for new members on how to handle borrowed saws. Part of the draft says: When you lay a saw on the workbench, make sure the blade is covered, and never leave it laying on the floor.

Which revision uses the correct verb?
options: When you lay a saw on the workbench, make sure the blade is covered, and never leave it lying on the floor.
When you lie a saw on the workbench, make sure the blade is covered, and never leave it lying on the floor.
When you lay a saw on the workbench, make sure the blade is covered, and never leave it laid on the floor.
When you lay a saw on the workbench, make sure the blade is covered, and never leave it lain on the floor.
items.explanation: Lay takes a direct object, as in lay a saw, so the first verb is correct. Lie means to rest in place, and its present participle is lying, which suits an object resting on the floor. Laying wrongly needs an object, while laid and lain are past forms that do not fit never leave it.

items.stem:
A newcomer to Birchfield wrote a thank-you note to the tool swap after borrowing a wheelbarrow. She asked a neighbor to check her draft. The note includes: Their was a long line at the hall, but the volunteers where friendly and quick.

Which revision corrects both commonly confused words?
options: There was a long line at the hall, but the volunteers where friendly and quick.
Their was a long line at the hall, but the volunteers were friendly and quick.
They’re was a long line at the hall, but the volunteers wear friendly and quick.
There was a long line at the hall, but the volunteers were friendly and quick.
items.explanation: There introduces the existence of a line, while their shows possession. Were is the past tense of be, while where refers to place. The key fixes both. The other options fix only one error or introduce new ones, such as they’re, a contraction of they are, and wear, a verb meaning to dress in.

items.stem:
The Birchfield tool swap posts summaries of each session so members who missed it can catch up. One summary excerpt reads: We collected forty hand tools, we repaired nine of them on the spot, and we sent the rest to the cleaning table.

Which choice best describes the punctuation of this sentence?
options: It is correct because commas separate three items in a series.
It is a comma splice because each clause needs a semicolon.
It is a run-on because it has no coordinating conjunction.
It is a fragment because the final clause lacks a subject.
items.explanation: Three independent clauses may be joined in a series, with commas between them and a conjunction before the last item, which this sentence has. Each clause has its own subject and verb, so it is not a fragment. A comma splice joins only two clauses with a comma and no conjunction.

items.stem:
The Calder Street bridge reopens next month after two years of repairs. A city engineer drafted the update for the town website. One sentence reads: Beneath the new deck sits the original stone piers, which engineers decided to keep.

Which revision corrects the sentence?
options: Beneath the new deck sits the original stone piers, which engineers decided to keep.
Beneath the new deck sit the original stone piers, which engineers decided to keep.
Beneath the new deck sit the original stone pier, which engineers decided to keep.
Beneath the new deck sits the original stone piers which engineers decided to keep.
items.explanation: In this inverted sentence the subject, piers, comes after the verb, so the verb must be plural: sit. The draft keeps a singular verb for a plural subject. The other choices leave the verb singular or change piers to pier, or remove the comma before the nonessential clause.

items.stem:
The Calder Street bridge project issued a notice to drivers about closures during the final week. The draft says: The bridge will close at 9 p.m., and the detour begins at the Mill Road intersection, which is marked with orange signs, drivers should plan an extra ten minutes.

Which choice best identifies the error in the draft?
options: The last clause is joined to the others with only a comma, making a run-on.
The clause which is marked with orange signs should not have commas.
The abbreviation p.m. should be written as a full word.
The word extra should be changed to extras.
items.explanation: The final clause, drivers should plan an extra ten minutes, is a separate sentence that is joined to the earlier material by only a comma, creating a run-on. The clause with which is nonessential and correctly set off. The abbreviation and the word extra are acceptable as written.

items.stem:
A reporter covering the Calder Street bridge reopening is writing about the ribbon cutting. Her draft reads: Hoping to avoid the crowd at the ceremony, the new walkway was used by Ms. Pruitt early in the morning.

Which revision corrects the misplaced modifier?
options: Hoping to avoid the crowd at the ceremony, the new walkway was a good choice for Ms. Pruitt early in the morning.
Hoping to avoid the crowd at the ceremony, early in the morning Ms. Pruitt’s use of the new walkway happened.
Hoping to avoid the crowd at the ceremony, the new walkway early in the morning was used by Ms. Pruitt.
Hoping to avoid the crowd at the ceremony, Ms. Pruitt used the new walkway early in the morning.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes a person, but the draft names the walkway right after the comma. Placing Ms. Pruitt next to the phrase fixes the problem. The other choices still start with the walkway, a use, or a time, none of which can hope to avoid anything.

items.stem:
The Calder Street bridge is being praised in a local magazine for its design. The article compares the old bridge with the new one. The sentence in the draft reads: The new bridge is wider than the old bridge, and it is more safer for cyclists.

Which revision corrects the comparison?
options: The new bridge is wider than the old bridge, and it is more safer for cyclists than before.
The new bridge is more wider than the old bridge, and it is safer for cyclists.
The new bridge is wider than the old bridge, and it is safer for cyclists.
The new bridge is wider than the old bridge, and it is most safe for cyclists.
items.explanation: Safer is already a comparative form, so adding more creates a double comparative. The key removes more and keeps the sentence parallel. The other options keep more safer, add more to wider, or switch to most safe, which is a superlative form that is not suited to comparing two bridges.

items.stem:
A school principal near the Calder Street bridge is writing a brief letter to parents about the reopening. She wants to point out how the bridge will change the walk to school. Her draft says: The bridge reopening is going to make a big difference to students, therefore, the walk will take half as long.

Which revision punctuates the sentence correctly?
options: The bridge reopening is going to make a big difference to students, therefore the walk will take half as long.
The bridge reopening is going to make a big difference to students; therefore, the walk will take half as long.
The bridge reopening is going to make a big difference to students therefore, the walk will take half as long.
The bridge reopening is going to make a big difference to students; therefore the walk, will take half as long.
items.explanation: Therefore is a conjunctive adverb joining two complete clauses, so it takes a semicolon before it and a comma after it. The draft with commas on both sides makes a comma splice. The other choices drop the semicolon or the comma, or put a stray comma between walk and its verb.

items.stem:
A school science club plans to launch a weather balloon from the Ridgemont athletic field. The club advisor wrote a permission letter to families. One sentence reads: The students who builds the sensor packs is excited to see the readings.

Which revision corrects the sentence?
options: The students who builds the sensor packs are excited to see the readings.
The students who build the sensor packs is excited to see the readings.
The student who build the sensor packs are excited to see the readings.
The students who build the sensor packs are excited to see the readings.
items.explanation: The subject students is plural, and the relative pronoun who takes a plural verb, build. The main verb must also be plural, are. The other choices fix only one of the two verbs, or change the subject to a singular noun while leaving plural verbs.

items.stem:
The Ridgemont weather balloon launch will be recorded in the science club’s logbook. A student wrote the entry before the event. It reads: The balloon rose steadily until it reached ten thousand feet, where the air pressure dropped, and the balloon will burst as planned.

Which revision keeps the tense consistent with the rest of the narration?
options: The balloon rose steadily until it reached ten thousand feet, where the air pressure dropped, and the balloon burst as planned.
The balloon rose steadily until it reaches ten thousand feet, where the air pressure dropped, and the balloon burst as planned.
The balloon rose steadily until it reached ten thousand feet, where the air pressure drops, and the balloon bursts as planned.
The balloon rises steadily until it reached ten thousand feet, where the air pressure dropped, and the balloon burst as planned.
items.explanation: The events are narrated in the past tense: rose, reached, dropped. The last verb, will burst, shifts to the future without reason, so burst is needed. The other choices introduce present tense verbs into a past narrative, reaches, drops, or rises, which break the sequence.

items.stem:
Before the Ridgemont weather balloon launches, the club prints a safety card. A volunteer wrote: Students should wait behind the rope, they must not touch the balloon, and adults will hold the lines.

Which revision fixes the punctuation without changing the meaning?
options: Students should wait behind the rope, they must not touch the balloon; and adults will hold the lines.
Students should wait behind the rope; they must not touch the balloon, and adults will hold the lines.
Students should wait behind the rope they must not touch the balloon, and adults will hold the lines.
Students should wait behind the rope, however they must not touch the balloon, and adults will hold the lines.
items.explanation: A semicolon can join two related independent clauses. The draft joins the first two with only a comma, which is a comma splice. The second choice puts the semicolon in the wrong place, the third has no break at all, and the fourth adds however without a semicolon, so the splice remains.

items.stem:
The Ridgemont science club is writing a news release about its weather balloon project. The club president wants the release to sound professional. Her draft says: Our balloon is gonna go way up high and take a bunch of cool pictures of the clouds.

Which revision best fits the formal tone of a news release?
options: Our balloon is going to go really high and take lots of neat pictures of the clouds.
Our balloon is going to climb way up and grab a bunch of cool cloud photos.
Our balloon will ascend to a high altitude and photograph the cloud formations.
Our balloon will go up high and take tons of awesome pictures of the sky.
items.explanation: A news release calls for precise, formal wording. Ascend to a high altitude and photograph the cloud formations replace slang such as gonna, way up, and cool. The other options keep casual expressions such as really high, lots of neat, grab a bunch, and tons of awesome, which weaken the formal tone.

items.stem:
A teacher is reviewing a student’s field report on the Ridgemont weather balloon. The student described the equipment list. The sentence reads: The package contained a camera, a thermometer, a battery pack, and it also had a small GPS tracker.

Which revision makes the list parallel?
options: The package contained a camera, a thermometer, a battery pack, and also had a small GPS tracker.
The package contained a camera, a thermometer, a battery pack, and then a small GPS tracker that it had.
The package contained a camera, a thermometer, a battery pack, plus there was a small GPS tracker.
The package contained a camera, a thermometer, a battery pack, and a small GPS tracker.
items.explanation: Items in a series should have the same form. A camera, a thermometer, a battery pack, and a small GPS tracker are all noun phrases. The other options end the list with a verb phrase, a longer clause, or a new sentence pattern, so the last item does not match the others.

items.stem:
A bookbinding workshop at the Fenwick arts center teaches beginners to sew signatures into a hardcover book. The instructor wrote a supply list for the registration page. One sentence reads: Each student should bring there own bone folder, needle, and waxed thread.

Which word should replace there?
options: their
they’re
them
theirs
items.explanation: Their is the possessive form meaning belonging to them, which is needed before own. There is a place word, they’re is a contraction of they are, and theirs stands alone without a noun after it. Only their works before the phrase own bone folder, because the students are the owners of the tools they bring to the class.

items.stem:
A bookbinding student at Fenwick wrote about her first book for the workshop blog. She asked a friend to look at one sentence: Folding the paper carefully, the spine of the book was sewn by Imogen with linen thread.

Which revision corrects the dangling modifier?
options: Folding the paper carefully, the spine of the book was sewn with linen thread by Imogen.
Folding the paper carefully, the spine was sewn by Imogen with linen thread.
Folding the paper carefully, Imogen sewed the spine of the book with linen thread.
Folding the paper carefully, Imogen’s sewing of the spine used linen thread.
items.explanation: The phrase folding the paper carefully must describe a person, so Imogen has to follow the comma. The first two choices still put the spine as the subject, which cannot fold paper. The last choice makes the sewing the subject, which also cannot fold, so only the key fixes the problem.

items.stem:
The Fenwick bookbinding instructor posted guidance on choosing glue for beginners. A sentence in the draft reads: Paste made from wheat starch is more flexible and holds longer then regular white glue.

Which word fixes the error?
options: that
than
when
as
items.explanation: A comparison with more flexible and holds longer needs than. Then refers to time. That, when, and as do not complete the comparison of paste with white glue. Than correctly introduces the second item being compared, here the regular white glue, so the sentence reads clearly and matches the comparison the instructor intends for beginners.

items.stem:
A Fenwick workshop student wrote a review of the bookbinding class for the arts center’s website. One sentence reads: The instructor, who’s patience never wore thin, answered every question about the spine.

Which revision corrects the error?
options: The instructor, whose patience never wore thin, answered every question about the spine.
The instructor, whose’ patience never wore thin, answered every question about the spine.
The instructor who’s patience never wore thin answered every question about the spine.
The instructor, who is patience never wore thin, answered every question about the spine.
items.explanation: Whose is the possessive form of who and shows that the patience belongs to the instructor. Who’s is a contraction of who is, which does not make sense here. The other choices add a stray apostrophe, remove the commas, or expand the contraction to who is, so the error remains.

items.stem:
The Fenwick arts center is hosting an exhibit of handmade books. The program note is being edited for concision. The draft says: The finished books, each one completed by hand, are all completely handmade and entirely made by individual makers.

Which revision best removes redundancy?
options: The finished books, each one completed by hand, are made by individual makers.
The finished books are all completely handmade and entirely made by hand.
The finished books are completely handmade and entirely made by individual makers.
The finished books are all handmade by individual makers.
items.explanation: Handmade already means made by hand, so completely handmade and entirely made repeat the idea. The key keeps handmade and by individual makers once each. The other options keep two phrases that say the same thing, such as by hand with handmade, or completely with entirely.

items.stem:
The Harlow College career fair posted a feedback form for employers and students. A staff member drafted a line for the results page. It reads: There were less employers at this year’s fair than last year, but the line at each booth was longer.

Which word should replace less?
options: lesser
fewer
least
few
items.explanation: Employers can be counted, so the comparison needs fewer. Less is used with amounts that cannot be counted, such as time or traffic. Lesser means smaller in importance, least is a superlative, and few does not fit a comparison with the phrase than last year.

items.stem:
A coordinator at the Eastgate library is pairing tutors with students who need extra help. She wrote an email to a volunteer. The draft says: Please tell me whom you would like to work with, and I will contact the student who’s schedule matches yours.

Which revision corrects the remaining error?
options: Please tell me who you would like to work with, and I will contact the student whose schedule matches yours.
Please tell me whom you would like to work with, and I will contact the student, whose schedule, matches yours.
Please tell me whom you would like to work with, and I will contact the student whose schedule matches yours.
Please tell me whom you would like to work with, and I will contact the student who is schedule matches yours.
items.explanation: Whose shows possession, so it belongs before schedule. Whom is already correct as the object of work with. The other choices change whom to who, add commas that interrupt an essential clause, or expand the contraction to who is, which is not grammatical in the sentence.

items.stem: A Marlow composting pilot volunteer is helping a neighbor write a letter to the council. The letter describes a conversation about bins. Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
options: “Will the bins be collected on Fridays”? Mr. Hale asked, “or has the schedule changed?”
“Will the bins be collected on Fridays?” Mr. Hale asked, “or has the schedule changed?”
“Will the bins be collected on Fridays?”, Mr. Hale asked “or has the schedule changed”?
“Will the bins be collected on Fridays,” Mr. Hale asked, “or has the schedule changed?”
items.explanation: A question mark that belongs to the quoted question goes inside the closing quotation marks. After the speaker tag, a comma sets off the rest of the quotation, which ends with its own question mark inside the marks. The other choices misplace the question mark or add commas that do not belong.

items.stem:
The Tern Point erosion study held a public meeting to share early results. A volunteer drafted this line for the meeting handout: Because the cliff has lost two meters of soil since 2022.

Which choice best revises the line to correct the fragment?
options: Because the cliff has lost two meters of soil since 2022, and the town is concerned.
The cliff has lost two meters of soil since 2022, because.
The town is concerned because the cliff has lost two meters of soil since 2022.
Because the cliff has lost two meters of soil since 2022; the town is concerned.
items.explanation: The draft begins with because, so it is a dependent clause that cannot stand alone. Placing it after a main clause, the town is concerned, completes the idea. The other choices keep the dependent clause alone, end with because, or connect it with a semicolon, which is for independent clauses.

items.stem:
The Pelham Quay tram society is writing a thank-you for two helpers who restored the tram’s window frames. The editor is checking a sentence. It reads: The two volunteers’ skill with the plane and chisel, impressed the visiting inspector.

Which revision corrects the punctuation error?
options: The two volunteers’ skill with the plane and chisel impressed the visiting inspector.
The two volunteers skill with the plane and chisel, impressed the visiting inspector.
The two volunteer’s skill with the plane and chisel impressed the visiting inspector.
The two volunteers’ skill, with the plane and chisel, impressed the visiting inspector.
items.explanation: A comma should not separate the subject, skill, from its verb, impressed. The apostrophe after volunteers is correct because there are two volunteers who share the skill. The other choices remove the apostrophe, use a singular possessive, or add commas that set off an essential phrase.
